entries.title: 8 Best Computer Speakers (2026) After Testing 30 Pairs
entries.summary: After testing 30 pairs of computer speakers, these are the best computer speakers—from stereo speakers to subwoofers to surround sound systems.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

Good computer speakers can make for a quick desktop upgrade. Sound is often overlooked when people buy a PC. Some folks prefer headphones, others stick with those old, battered speakers they inherited, and some rely on the awful built-in speaker in their monitor. With any of the speakers in this list, you can enhance voices in video calls and movies, tease out greater depth in your favorite music, and provide spatial awareness in games. After several months of testing, I've narrowed my selection across various budgets and preferences. Whether you want a soundbar for your computer, a pair of speakers, or a surround sound system, you can find it here.

Be sure to check out our many other audio guides, like the Best Soundbars, Best Bluetooth Speakers, Best Wireless Headphones, Best Gaming Headsets, and Best Bookshelf Speakers.

Updated November 2026: I added speakers from Creative, a mention for speakers from Pioneer, and updated prices.

Other Computer Speakers I Liked

There are tons of computer speakers on the market, and many of the ones I tested are perfectly fine, but don't deserve a spot above for one reason or another.

Pioneer DJ DM-40D-BT for $239: Designed as entry-level speakers for bedroom DJs, the Pioneer DJ DM-40D-BTs sport a molded black plastic front with an MDF cabinet, but they feel well-built and solid. There’s a 4-inch fiberglass woofer with a 0.75-inch soft‑dome tweeter, and a class‑D amplifier with DSP (digital signal processing). Input options are RCA, 3.5-mm stereo mini, or Bluetooth 5.0, with a 3.5-mm headphone port in front, a simple volume knob, and a Bluetooth button. On the back of the control speaker, there’s a DJ/Production switch, which dials up the boomy bass. The sound quality is decent for the money, but they’re a bit too big for my desktop. If you need a budget option for music production to pair with a laptop, they might be a good shout, though the IK Multimedia iLoud Micro Monitors above are better if you can find the extra cash.

Edifier M60 for $200: Close to matching my top picks in sound quality, but significantly cheaper, the Edifier M60 speakers produce a rich, clear sound that persists when you crank the volume. The bass is decent, considering the lack of a subwoofer, but it can get muddy and a bit rattly. You have three connection options, including USB-C, 3.5 mm, or Bluetooth 5.3. My test music playlist sounded great on these speakers, and only the rumbly bass distracted me in games and movies, though they come with angled stands that point them at your ears and reduce vibrations. The M60 speakers are also the perfect size for most desktops. On the downside, the touch controls are a little annoying (you have to hold down for three seconds to power on/off or change mode), and the Edifier ConneX app for Android (also available on iOS) was a little flaky, though it offered some handy customization options and a six-band equalizer. Overall, these speakers are a solid option if this is your budget.

Creative Pebble Nova for $266: These eye-catching orb-shaped speakers with RGB rings around the base are a statement piece for your desk. They are big, angled at 45 degrees, and you have the choice of a flat base or elevated stands. They light up, produce a pleasant sound that’s rich across the board and with real depth, and can, frankly, get far too loud for your desktop. I was also impressed by the virtual surround sound for gaming. Don’t make the mistake of thinking the Creative App is superfluous, because it’s packed with options, from an equalizer to dialogue enhancement to RGB lighting controls. While I love the stand, it made them too tall for my desk because of my dual monitors. I also found the touch controls a bit finicky, and I advise switching off the power saving mode.

Ruark MR1 MK3 for $599: Perfect for a retro vibe, the styling includes a fabric front, and black finish with a dial on top. With a fluid and expansive soundstage, music sounds great on these speakers, and even without a subwoofer, there’s a decent rumble of bass. I found Ruark’s speakers equally pleasing for watching movies and video calls, as voice clarity is excellent, though I experienced some slight distortion with deep voices during meetings. They are also quite large, maybe too large for some desks.

OXS Thunder Pro for $600: With a compact design, sci-fi styling that includes RGB lighting, and no separate subwoofer, I was unsure what to expect from this soundbar. The Thunder Pro is 24 inches long and just 3 inches tall, so slotted into place perfectly under my monitor. It comes with a wired control dial, a remote control, and extra feet in the box to angle it. I was immediately impressed when the bass of Dead Prez’s “Hip-Hop” kicked in, bouncing the passive radiators up and down. The sound is expansive, the bass is far better than it has any right to be without a large subwoofer, and the highs are surprisingly crisp. This soundbar is Dolby Atmos-certified and has three distinct gaming modes. The first-person shooter mode offered excellent spatial sound, allowing me to hear the footsteps and grunts of a cloaked Elite in Halo Infinite just in time to avoid being impaled. Connectivity is comprehensive with USB-A and USB-C, 3.5-mm aux, Bluetooth 5.0, two HDMI ports (one eARC), a mic-in port, and a headphone jack. All that’s missing is the option to hook up a subwoofer. The wired control unit lights up, acts as a volume dial and power button, and has EQ and mode buttons on the back. While the OXS Thunder Pro impressed, you will get better sound, especially for music, if you buy separate speakers and a subwoofer.

Razer Nommo V2 Pro for $438: Stick to one brand for all your gaming gear, and it’s easier to achieve harmony. Plus, you only need one app to configure everything. If Razer is your jam, the Nommo V2 Pro is a 2.1 system with tempting bells and whistles. These stylish cylindrical speakers fire light out the back and tilt up towards your ears. The chunky subwoofer is wireless, which could be handy if you prefer to keep the space under your desk free. The wireless control puck acts as a volume dial, and you can press it to mute, play, or skip. You can expect booming bass and rich mids, but there’s a little crispness lacking in the highs, particularly when you crank the volume up. The sound profile is well-suited to action movies and games, with a deep bass rumble that you feel in the pit of your stomach. Connectivity is limited to USB or Bluetooth 5.3. I had some setup issues with the wireless control puck, but after a few attempts, the new firmware was installed successfully. I still found it a bit flaky and didn’t like having to hold it down to turn the speakers on. (They switch off automatically unless you deactivate the power-saving setting.) While Razer Chroma RGB now supports more than 300 games, offers various effects, and an ambient awareness mode that reacts to your screen, there are only two lighting zones (one for each speaker). Unfortunately, the Razer Synapse software is the only way to get at some settings, and it feels bloated and sometimes hogs system resources.

Logitech G560 Lightsync for $250: Folks who prefer Logitech gear should consider the G560 Lightsync. This 2.1 system comprises a huge subwoofer and two speakers with an attractive curved loop design. The speakers project RGB lighting onto the wall behind them. Sound-wise, the bass is dominant and the soundstage lacks definition, but you can play around with the equalizer or use the presets Logitech provides. For movies and gaming, the G560 does better, with DTS:X Ultra virtual surround sound to emulate larger systems. There’s a good thump of bass for explosions, and they provide a decent positional sense in games. These speakers connect via USB, but there’s also a 3.5-mm aux port and support for Bluetooth 4.1. Sadly, for lighting fans, you only get four zones of LEDs here, but there are lots of presets and colors to choose from, and you can have them react to the onscreen action. While these speakers don’t grab me, with the bass bossing the show, they are decent value, particularly as the price has dropped significantly since they were first released.

SteelSeries Arena 7 for $380: The SteelSeries Arena 7 boasts great sound and real versatility. This 2.1 system is the sweet spot in the SteelSeries Arena lineup, as it adds a chunky subwoofer and RGB lighting over the Arena 3, but is still relatively affordable. Simply plug in the USB and attach the pear-shaped speakers to the subwoofer. The adjustable speakers look interesting, with RGB lighting around the base and back, and a mode button and volume dial on the right speaker (headphone port behind it). This system produces a soundstage with clarity and precision, but can sound too bassy and flat, though you can tweak it in the SteelSeries GG software. The spatial sound for games is immersive and accurate enough to help you pinpoint footsteps or the whomp of an approaching helicopter. With USB, Bluetooth 4.2, optical in and out, and 3.5-mm aux, your connectivity bases are covered. You can also sync the Prism RGB lighting with the rest of your setup, have it react to music, or just pick a color. On the downside, the speakers are quite tall, and the subwoofer is bulky and sometimes overpowers the sound.

Majority DX10 Desktop Speakers for £13: They lack bass and general clarity, but these USB-powered speakers are the cheapest I’ve tried. These 10-watt, 2.5-inch, full-range speakers are angled up toward your ears and have a simple power and volume dial. There’s also a 3.5 mm headphone port. Only available in the UK, they could be enough if your budget is very tight.

Edifier G2000 Pro for $212: A spruced-up version of the G2000 above, the Pro is an upgrade to 64-watt power, 3-inch full-range drivers, and virtual 7.1 surround sound. Edifier also made these speakers translucent and added garish RGB lighting effects courtesy of LED strips in each speaker. They do sound a bit better, though still lacking in bass, and some folks will love the sci-fi light show, but there isn’t enough extra to justify the significant jump in price.

Creative Pebble X Plus for $123: If our budget pick isn’t quite doing it for you, Creative’s Pebble X Plus adds a cube-shaped subwoofer under your desk. The larger speakers, with RGB lighting, are also more powerful, and the sub provides punchy bass. They sound reasonably good for the money. Connectivity is also beefed up compared to the V3 above, with headphone and microphone ports and Bluetooth 5.3, but all of this invariably comes at a higher cost.

Onkyo Creator GX-10DB for $250: Capable of producing a warm and rich sound, Onkyo’s speakers are the perfect size for your desktop and come with angled stands (though they are plastic). The connectivity options are solid, with USB-C, optical, and stereo RCA inputs, and support for Bluetooth 5.3. These speakers get a little louder than our top pick, though you’ll need to pair a subwoofer if you’re into bass (there is a subwoofer-out port). Sadly, the volume knob on the back of the right speaker is tricky to reach, the slim remote control has a weird layout, and the source LED on the front is always on. But what I struggled with most was the automatic power-off (Onkyo says this “feature” is an eco-regulation in Europe) that turns off the speakers if they aren’t used for 15 minutes. If you have more space and crave more power, I also tested the Onkyo Creator Series GX-30ARC ($350), which goes far louder and adds a decent thump of bass.

Creative Sound Blaster GS5 for $95: While it doesn’t quite have the power of the OXS Thunder Lite above, this soundbar is cheaper and matches it on connectivity, even adding cool RGB lighting to the underside. It also has a remote and decent software for making EQ and lighting adjustments. The sound lacks clarity, and the bass is limited, but this is a solid, small soundbar for the money and works well as a desktop device.

Logitech Z407 for $110: A complete 2.1 system at this price is no mean feat. These speakers connect via USB, 3.5-mm aux, or Bluetooth, and there’s a wireless remote volume dial. Construction is cheap, and the sound lacks definition, but there’s a good thump of bass from the subwoofer, and mids and highs are reasonably crisp, provided you don’t turn the volume up too high. WIRED senior reviews editor Julian Chokkattu says he used a variation of the Logitech Z-series for nearly a decade and only recently donated them to someone else.

Razer Nommo V2 X for $150: The sound quality of Razer’s entry-level speakers is solid for music and good for movies and games (there's THX Spatial support), though lacking in bass. These no-frills speakers look great but lack a subwoofer, RGB lighting, and a remote. They offer USB and Bluetooth connectivity and can be customized in Razer’s Synapse software.

The PC Speakers I Don't Recommend

These are the computer speakers that had deal-breaking flaws for me.

OXS Thunder Duo X for $550: These powerful speakers get plenty loud and come with a wireless neck speaker for surround sound, but they are very large (way too big for my desk) and, frankly, kinda garish when they light up. The sound quality is decent and I liked the surround sound for gaming, but the neck speaker is not comfortable, especially for long gaming sessions (much will depend on your office chair). You can also get these speakers with a subwoofer.

OXS Thunder Lite for $150: This compact soundbar lacks the bells and whistles of its bigger sibling above, but is far more affordable. It can get plenty loud, supports virtual surround sound, and comes with a small remote. Unfortunately, separation was poor, so it was tough to tell where sounds were coming from in games, and it is severely lacking in bass for a soundbar with thunder in its name. Connectivity includes USB-C, 3.5-mm aux, optical, or HDMI, and it supports Bluetooth 5.0.

Edifier QR65 for $314: Delivering classy looks with supercool lighting effects and a seriously big, powerful sound, these speakers are excellent for music, movies, or games. They also come with two angled stands to point them at your ears. They have USB, RCA, and Bluetooth 5.3 connectivity and USB ports for charging your gadgets. Controls are decent, with a physical button on the right speaker for power and cycling through modes. The problem is that they are huge and won’t fit on most desktops, including mine.

Creative Stage V2 for $150: This affordable soundbar offers excellent connectivity with HDMI ARC, optical, USB, 3.5-mm aux, and Bluetooth 5.0. But it’s not especially powerful, can sound muddy and flat, and has a short cable (no good for sit-stand desks). The subwoofer lends some decent bass, there’s a remote control, and I like the Clear Dialog option to sharpen voices, but you can do better.

House of Marley Get Together Duo for $170: Sporting an attractive and eco-friendly blend of bamboo and fabric, the Get Together Duo from House of Marley is affordable. They connect via Bluetooth 5.0, RCA, or 3.5-mm aux. There’s no subwoofer, the midrange is dominant, and they are lacking something at the high end. The battery-powered right speaker can also double as a portable speaker, and you can use these as bookshelf speakers, but as computer speakers, they are just OK.

SteelSeries Arena 3 for $150: Sporting a nice pear-shaped design with tiltable speakers and subtle branding, the entry-level Arena 3 from SteelSeries can get loud. But they lack bass, lose detail in the highs, and sound a bit fuzzy for music. Even for SteelSeries fans, there isn’t much reason to choose these over some of our picks above. They don’t have lighting, USB, or any other extras.

Logitech Z906 5.1 Surround Sound Speaker System for $450: This 5.1 system is THX-certified and comes with a huge subwoofer, five speakers, and a central control unit. The design feels dated, maybe even a bit ugly, and you need to run cables around your room. The surround sound effect is solid, and you can even convert stereo with the 3D mode, but overall, it’s a bass-heavy system.

Are Computer Speakers Worth It?

Budget is a deciding factor for most folks, but even cheap desktop speakers offer far better sound than your monitor. Headphones are a great alternative, but not everyone wants to wear headphones all the time. You can spend as much as you like on audio gear, but I have focused on reasonably affordable desktop systems here, starting from as low as $35 and not exceeding $700.

What Should I Look for in Computer Speakers?

It depends. There’s plenty to weigh when shopping for a set of computer speakers, so it’s vital to start by deciding what’s most important to you. For example, I work and play on the same desktop PC, so I need speakers that perform well for video calls, long gaming sessions, listening to music, and watching movies. I also have a standing desk, and my monitor setup doesn’t leave much room, so I prefer compact all-rounders with long cables.

Sound quality: The top consideration for most folks, you want the best sound quality you can afford. A good set of speakers will offer a balance of clear vocals, rich treble, and rumbling bass. If you crave bass you feel in the pit of your stomach, a subwoofer is essential, though it might not be a good idea for folks who have downstairs neighbors. For accurate positional sound, you might want to look at a surround sound system with multiple speakers.

Design: Consider the finish. Your speakers will be on show, so you’ll want to pick something that fits your decor.

Brand: Gamers with devices from an existing brand might lean toward the same brand of speakers because they can be configured in the same software. This is particularly important with speakers that have built-in lights, so you can sync up your entire setup.

Extras: Some people will consider these superfluous, but if you want a remote control for kicking back or RGB lighting to bring a splash of color to your desk, these are extra perks on higher-end speakers. Snag speakers with a decent range of connectivity, and you can always repurpose them later. Most speakers come with all the cables you need, but it’s worth checking before you buy. I have listed what you will find in the box with all the computer speakers I recommend.

Where Should I Position My Desktop Speakers?

You ideally want the speakers to be angled slightly up (around 15 degrees) and pointed at your ears. Since you know the exact spot you’ll be in when listening, you can tweak the position of your speakers for the best results. Don’t just chuck them on the desk and leave it at that. Try moving and angling them until you find that sweet spot.

Do I Need Speaker Stands?

Speaker stands can maximize sound quality by helping to reduce vibrations from your desktop that can muddy the sound. Angled speaker stands are also a good way to direct the sound toward your ears. Some manufacturers, such as Edifier and Onkyo, include stands; IK Multimedia and Razer include adjustable bases or fold-out feet; Audioengine sells stands separately. You will also find a wide choice of third-party stands online.

What Size Speakers Should I Get?

If space is limited, a compact set of speakers will work best. The trade-off is power and volume, as small speakers generally don’t produce as big or high-quality a sound as large speakers. If you opt for a subwoofer, you will want a suitable space under your desk. For surround sound systems, you must run cables and find suitable spots for speakers behind you. If you have a wide monitor on a mount, a compact soundbar beneath it could be the best fit. Check the dimensions carefully and measure the space on your desk before you buy.

What’s the Best Way to Connect My Speakers to My Computer?

Speakers can come with a multitude of ports and connectivity options. USB connections usually sound best because they output the digital signal for the digital-to-analog converter (DAC) in the speakers, which is likely to be better unless you have a good sound card. But the best way to be sure is to try both and see which sounds better. If you want to be able to connect a phone or laptop wirelessly, then Bluetooth is paramount. Most speakers have a 3.5-mm aux input, and some have an output for headphones. Just make sure your preferred speakers support the connectivity you want. You should also make sure that you have the necessary free ports on your PC or laptop, though you can always add more with a USB hub.

How I Test Computer Speakers

Every set of speakers in this guide was tested for at least a week, sometimes longer. I don’t use headphones, so they were all used for video calls throughout my work day, listening to music and podcasts, and for movies and games in the evening. While I played several games, watched many movies or shows, and listened to lots of music and podcasts, I ran through a specific list of test content with every speaker system to make it easier to compare them.

My test content included the game Halo Infinite, the movie Dune, and a music playlist including “Hip-Hop” (Dead Prez), “The National Anthem” (Radiohead), “All Along the Watchtower” (Jimi Hendrix), “Hey” (Pixies), “Sabotage” (Beastie Boys), “A Day in the Life” (the Beatles), “Nothing Compares 2 U” (Sinéad O'Connor), and “Only God Knows” (Young Fathers).

entries.title: I Used NYT Cooking’s New AI-Powered Recipe Modifier, and It’s Actually Pretty Good
entries.summary: The New York Times has added a beta feature to its Cooking app that helps readers swap ingredients or adjust recipes to suit their needs. It mostly hits the mark.
entries.content:
In an aside in the New York Times Cooking video I watched recently, where Melissa Clark made her lemony white bean soup with turkey and greens, the food reporter and recipe columnist invited viewers to leave a comment telling her what they do with the kale stems. It highlighted this sweet, funny relationship between a media brand’s personalities and its audience, a warm-casual vibe.

I am not among the multitudes in the Cooking section's commenter army, but a few days later I was very surprised to see some of them in open revolt. I was even more surprised to see why: In an iOS-only beta, the Times is now using AI to allow subscribers to modify recipes.

Below the article announcing the change on October 23, commenters loudly aired their grievances, threatening to cancel subscriptions, asking who wanted this, and how to turn it off.

After four days and 172 almost exclusively angry comments, commenting for the story was turned off.

The Times doesn't share Cooking's subscriber numbers, but NYT executive communications director Jordan Cohen said the site and app were visited 514 million times in 2025, and its YouTube channel has over 1.4 million subscribers. Reading over the section's AI plans and thinking about how many bungled attempts I'd seen to mush technology into places where it doesn't need to be in the kitchen, I guessed that I would side with the commenters. Then I tried the new AI feature, and found that it worked surprisingly well.

My writing for WIRED over the past decade has shown me again and again that adding tech to a kitchen product is risky at best. I've repeatedly watched companies try and fail: Bluetooth connections for all the appliances, apps that lean too heavily on crummy recipes, toasters with optical sensors or touchscreens that still couldn't toast particularly well. Just about anything that was part of the "smart kitchen" tended not to be very smart at all.

Developing dependable, delicious recipes is hard, expensive work that can require a whole staff. Yet skimping can hurt the brand. Two notable companies with a deep bench—The New York Times Cooking and America's Test Kitchen—are cooking content makers. Recipes, which is to say delicious, high-quality, tested recipes, are what they do.

Since AI is often a lousy chef, giving it a role in the presentation of NYT's gold mine of content is a big risk.

Earlier this year, the Times allowed AI to help with a recipe-scaling feature (modifying ingredient quantities so "serves 4" turns into "serves 6") and converting from imperial measurements to metric—cups, tablespoons, and Fahrenheit to grams, milliliters, and Celsius. Now, in the iOS-only beta, a "customize this recipe" field appears just above the ingredient list.

If you want to make banana bread but tell it you don't have a loaf pan, it'll ask you what kind of pans you do have, then modify the recipe to suit. All the changes throughout the recipe are noted in a visible red-orange text. Over several days of testing, I saw how you can do relatively simple things like swap ground pork for ground beef, or make more complicated demands like asking it to tailor things to your dietary needs. The modifications it makes are very visible throughout the recipe. If you ask it for something too out there—like turning Eric Kim's gochujang buttered noodles into a cookie—it gives you a "hard redirect" and points you to a better-suited recipe, which in this case is Kim's gochujang caramel cookies.

"We put a lot of effort into trying to tell you when not to do something if it's no longer in the spirit of the recipe," says Camilla Velasquez, the general manager of NYT Cooking.

For its recommendations, the LLM looks at the recipe itself, the Times’ ingredient substitution guide, user comments, and then what it calls AI "drawing on our expertise," in that order. Velasquez says the AI should be a helper, not the main act, noting, "You shouldn't be chatting with it."

She explains that when the Times built the AI functionality, recipe editors helped create the original rule set, then evaluated how it worked at the end.

When I ask what this means for the jobs of 60 editors, writers, video journalists, and other employees—the team that creates the recipes people use and curates the vibe readers relate to—Velasquez stresses that NYT Cooking has been "hiring more than ever" and that it has "zero intention of publishing fewer recipes."

So far, she says people are mainly using it for ingredient and equipment substitutions, along with adjusting recipes for dietary needs. "Some people use the chatbot to scale, or they'll scale to match an ingredient," giving the example of someone who had only one cup of oil for a recipe that needed more.

As a food writer whose career has taken some substantial turns due to AI recently, I wouldn't say I've been clamoring for this, but I find the Times’ measured approach works pretty well.

I started testing it out by making chicken and dumplings using a five-star Alison Roman recipe with more than 6,000 ratings. I asked the AI tool to swap out bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs for boneless, skinless breasts. It thought about it for a moment—"simmering" in AI Cooking patois—and then offered up "Chicken Breast and Dumplings," with the "breast" in the title rendered in the red-orange color that indicates a modification. Just below the title, it said it was "Joseph's version made with AI. Not tested or endorsed by the original recipe's creators." Along with those visible changes, I could also toggle back and forth between my version and the original.

Once I started cooking, things went smoothly. I'm a recipe follower, not an improviser, and the Times’ recipes are easy to follow. The modifications were too. I was also impressed by how the app flagged that the chicken breast simmering time would be reduced because it cooks faster than thighs, and since they don't render as much fat as skin-on thighs do, it added some butter to the roux. These changes were incorporated into the right places in the recipe.

It all made sense except for one bit. It suggested the shredded, cooked breast go back into the pot for about another 30 minutes while the sauce thickens and the dumplings cook. I saw this coming and, well, I wasn't going to do that to my dinner. I put a handful of shredded meat in as directed so I could see what happened and reserved the rest. The shredded bits that were in for that extra half hour weren’t bad per se, but their texture was notably less succulent than what I'd reserved and way less than thighs would be.

This was the largest issue I encountered in all of my testing. If I had been the creator of the Times' original recipe, I'm not sure how I'd feel about the option to use a breast instead of thighs, which is not unheard of, but not very common in classic chicken and dumpling recipes. Perhaps it's something that could be fine-tuned or simply not offered as an option.

From there, it was fairly smooth sailing. I had it turn a Francis Lam roasted mushroom and broccoli grain bowl into a roasted mushroom, cauliflower, and squash grain bowl. The crucifer crisscross was an easy one-to-one, but I also told it to add a pound of delicata squash. It had me slice the squash into half moons so everything would finish at the same time, then upped the total amount of olive oil. Lam's poetic voice was preserved in both versions of the recipe, telling you to heat the olive oil "until it slips around the pan like water" before adding beaten eggs for festive dish-topping egg ribbons. My buddy Dave had come by for cribbage night, and this made for an enjoyable, healthy, pregame dinner before he went on to skunk me twice.

I'd been curious how it would handle batters, and it capably transformed Yewande Komolafe’s Toasted Sesame and Scallion Waffles into a yeasted version, which, unlike the original, gets an overnight in the fridge, letting the active dry yeast get bubbly and add an appealing tang.

A friend suggested Colu Henry's pasta and chickpea stew. I swapped canned diced tomatoes I had in my pantry for whole, and asked it to "add more vegetables." It gave options in line with the recipe—carrots, celery, onion, zucchini, mushrooms, and extra greens—then put what I chose into the right spots throughout the procedure so everything went in at the right time. It made for a healthy, hearty dinner.

Having been to the Portland Fermentation Festival recently and wanting guidance on incorporating a few extra ingredients, particularly garlic, into my sauerkraut, I used the AI to modify Lidey Heuck's original, saying "add carrots, garlic, and kale," which it suggested grating, thin slicing, and mincing, respectively, all in the right-feeling proportions. It also added more salt, since I was making more kraut. The big jar is sitting next to me as I type, and while it's several days from being ready, a sniff test tells me it's on its way to being a good batch.

Finally, I turned Sue Li's peanut noodles with spicy tofu into peanut udon with tofu, whitefish, and cucumber. I started by asking it to make the original less spicy, add veggies, and "keep the tofu," but add some good-looking rockfish I found at the grocery store. Impressively, since the fish was an add-on, it had me cook it, then set it aside and wipe out the pan (!) before cooking the tofu. Since I swapped udon for the original bucatini, it customized the noodle-cooking guidance, too.

It seems pretty natural that the Cooking section ran into some resistance when launching this feature. The NYT employs some of the best recipe creators in the business. Using AI to help us make substitutions is helpful, and the way the app integrates those changes into the recipes is impressive, but this tinkering with the original is essentially a subtractive process. How many of us are going to make substitutions and land on something better than Melissa Clark, Yewande Komolafe, or Francis Lam set out to make by design?

Instead, it's saving us a trip to the store, or helping us use something we have on hand, or making it gluten-free, serving as a good and rare example of how you can use technology to make a product incrementally better.

It also sounds like the commenters’ concerns have been heard. Velasquez let me know right away when we spoke that people will be able to hide the AI feature in the app if they want. The Times is also keeping the whole thing in iOS-only beta for now, and not saying when it would be available on other platforms.

That bond that you can see between the Cooking team and its users is a pretty sweet thing. Deep down, I'm guessing the upset Cooking commenters felt worried they were going to lose some of that human connection. I hope it never goes away.

entries.title: Wandrd’s Magnetic Camera Straps Are My New Favorite Accessory
entries.summary: More evidence that magnets are magical.
entries.content:
More than a decade ago, Peak Design rethought the humble camera strap. This was a necessary development. When you buy a camera, manufacturers almost always toss in a chintzy, uninspired strap with their logo on it. These cheap straps have cheap mounting systems that make it hard to quickly remove the strap from the camera when you need to, like when you're attaching your camera to a tripod or gimbal and you’d rather not have a dangling strap whacking you in the face.

Peak Design solved this with its Anchor Links system, small circular nubs you leave attached to camera eyelets that make detaching or even swapping straps easy. The quick-connect mechanism is now the de facto industry standard and has inspired countless copycats.

Now, Wandrd has outdone that design using magnets.

“We're photographers ourselves, so we're constantly ideating, tinkering, thinking of ways that things can be better,” Ryan Cope, Wandrd cofounder, tells WIRED. “A camera strap like this has been at the back of our minds for a while.”

Wandrd—known for its camera bags—launched its Magnetic Camera Strap system on Thursday. It features a circular anchor similar to Peak Design, called “Torus Links.” The anchors attach to your camera’s eyelets and are rated to carry up to 198 pounds—so unless you're bench-pressing your camera, they'll do the job. If the cord does start to wear down over time, you'll first see yellow under the black fabric—a sign you should replace the Torus Link. If it's red, you should stop using the link immediately—a warning system borrowed from Peak Design. (Wandrd offers a two-year warranty.)

Unlike Peak Design's anchors, the Wandrd anchors look like donuts, with a hole in the middle. When you attach the strap, the embedded magnets guide the Torus Link into the strap's CoreLock mechanism, which pinches into the hole to secure the camera body. The magnets make connecting a strap easier, and they keep the strap fastened to the anchor, but you can’t just pull the strap off like you’re pulling a MagSafe accessory on your phone. You’ll need to use the strap’s dual-pinch mechanism to remove it from the Torus Link, a design that’s more secure.

It’s a much faster way to connect and disconnect a strap, and that speed pays off in the field. This week, I had to photograph a product during a press briefing. Usually, I use Peak Design's Leash and, instead of taking off the strap, I bunch it up in my hand when it's not around my neck. It's not that it's hard to remove—it's just an extra step I have to think about. But Wandrd's magnetic system felt faster to unlock mid-shoot when I wanted to lower the camera for an awkward, low-angle shot, and reattaching the strap was practically instantaneous. I did the whole swap one-handed, with the magnets doing most of the work.

“I love magnets, man,” Cope says. “I love the simplicity they create—guiding things into place. You don't always have a place to put your camera down; I like that magnets help guide them and are a lot more secure, and they're also just fun.”

I have two Torus Links on my camera body, one on the right eyelet and another on the tripod baseplate. But my favorite configuration turns the strap into a single-point sling. The strap has a built-in “Torus Loop” on the buckle—clip one end directly into it to create a closed loop worn across your torso, leaving just a single magnetic connector to snap onto your camera. When you unclip the camera to shoot freely, the strap stays neatly in place across your body instead of sliding off your shoulder.

The nylon felt comfortable across my chest and near my neck—there's no padding, but that's intentional. Cope says Wandrd spent two years developing this custom “liquid nylon” tubular webbing that is softer along the edges, so it won't feel like the strap is cutting into your neck after a long day of wear. The lack of metal throughout the strap system also prevents the strap from scratching up your camera gear.

Best of all, you don't have to replace your strap to use Wandrd's system. If you have a strap you love—maybe a fancy leather strap someone gifted you—Wandrd is selling a DIY kit ($29) that lets you attach its Magnetic CoreLock system to the ends of your preferred strap. Otherwise, the strap kit comes in a 30-mm size ($69), a 15-mm “Lite" ($49), and a wrist strap ($39).

I don't know if Wandrd's system will see the same success as Peak Design's Anchor Links, but I don't see myself switching back anytime soon. Magnets are just too dang cool.

entries.title: How to Remind Your Boss of Your PTO Without Pissing Them Off
entries.summary: The next time you take paid time off, your boss and coworkers will remember if you follow this advice.
entries.content:
You're about to slam that laptop shut for two weeks when the boss messages, “See you Monday!”

We've all been there, staring down a manager who has forgotten about our paid time off—even though we told them!

When we communicate something that's important to us, we can forget that it's not necessarily as meaningful to the recipient. Surely you've been on the flip side, too, annoyed at a coworker who hasn't replied to your messages, until someone mentions that they're on holiday.

A key to efficient communication in the workplace is to repeat yourself. It sounds counterintuitive, but it's true. We're all better off when we overcommunicate by saying the same thing two or three times.

The trick is how and when you do it. Think of all the avenues you have for requesting, recording, and reminding people of your PTO. Use all the channels, and spread out the messaging so that each instance has relevant context and timing.

6 Weeks to 6 Months Out: Get It on the Books

If you like to plan in advance, you might request time off four to six months out. Not all managers appreciate this much notice, however, because they might not know what the workload will be when your vacation rolls around, making it hard for them to approve your dates.

How far in advance you should request time off is a conversation to have with your direct boss. It depends on them as a person, the type of work you do, the size of your team, and other factors. If this conversation doesn't give you much clarity, four to six weeks before your time off is probably about right. Start there and adjust as necessary.

Occasionally, you need approval well in advance for an event that cannot move and will cost you a lot of money to cancel, like your own wedding or a nonrefundable trip. In those cases, six months or more is not unreasonable, but bring it up from time to time so no one forgets.

Whenever you put in your initial request, it must be recorded. Log it into a time-off system if your organization uses one (human resources software, a shared calendar) or write it in an email with a clear subject line, and make sure your boss replies saying it's approved.

2 Weeks Out: Verbal Reminders

About two weeks before your time off, remind your boss and colleagues verbally in meetings. The ideal settings are in a weekly one-on-one meeting with your direct manager and in a team meeting.

Save your info for the end of the meeting after all pressing business has been discussed. If you need to make sure your responsibilities are covered while you're out, raise that point privately with your manager rather than in a team meeting so the boss has time to decide how to handle it.

1 Week Out: Email or Message Your Contacts

If you need to tell someone beyond your team—such as clients or another department—about your planned time off, do so in writing a week before you leave. This gives them plenty of opportunity to reach out while you’re still available.

Email is fine, though if you usually communicate with these people through Slack or Microsoft Teams, that may be a better option. How you format the message matters—see the next step for tips.

2 Business Days Out: Send Formatted Messages

Two business days before your time off begins, send a short, clear message to everyone who needs to know that you will be out. If the norm is to use Slack or Microsoft Teams, use that.

How you format this message makes a huge difference. The first sentence should say something like, "Just a reminder, I will be out beginning DATE. I will be back on DATE." This sentence can be in bold. The second DATE is the day you return to work, not the last day of your PTO. What's relevant to your colleagues is the day you are available.

If you need to give more information, such as who is covering for you, put that in a new paragraph. Do not go overboard with detail. It will make people crazy. Should you need to leave detailed instructions, put them in a shared document and link to it.

Why send this message two business days out? Simple: If your first PTO day is Monday, you send this message on Thursday so that anybody who takes off or calls in sick on Friday still sees it in time.

The Day You Leave: Set Your Status

My favorite PTO reminder is the status indicator in a team messaging platform. Set it to show you're out and add an appropriate emoji, like a palm tree or airplane.

Even if you dislike emoji, they are extremely efficient and effective communicators here. At a glance, everyone who sees it is reminded that you're out.

You can typically set a status message too; use this to tell everyone the date you’ll be available again.

Your First Day Off: A Final Reminder for the Extra Forgetful

For those supremely forgetful bosses and coworkers, you might set up an automated message that appears at 8:30 am the first day you're out. Slack, Teams, email, or even a text message will do the trick. Be concise. Be kind. And have a sense of humor. The point of the message is to be helpful—not make someone else feel like a forgetful jerk.

entries.title: A 55-Year-Old Math Problem Was Solved—This Time by Humans
entries.summary: A group of young mathematicians found the solution to the long unanswered conjecture, first inspired by juggling, through randomness and friendship.
entries.content:
The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.

The late Ronald Graham wore two hats. He was a renowned mathematician and, at one time, president of the American Mathematical Society. He was also a serious juggler and president of the International Jugglers’ Association. “He loved tricks,” said Fan Chung, a mathematician at UC San Diego who was married to Graham. “You know, spinning a ball, spinning a coat hanger, spinning several balls together, throwing pens against the wall.”

Sometimes Graham wore both hats at once. “It’s interesting, in fact, that many mathematicians and computer scientists have an interest in juggling,” he said in a 1980 television interview. “I think it’s the search for patterns and structure that is responsible for this.”

He would go on to write numerous papers, some with Chung, on the mathematics of juggling. But back in 1971, decades before he made that connection explicit, he posed a question that some mathematicians now say might have been inspired by juggling, too.

Start with a random set of different integers, not including zero. Can you always rearrange them so that if you add up the first two numbers, then the first three, then the first four, and so on, every “partial sum” turns out different? In the language of juggling, this would mean that if each ball stays in the air for a different amount of time, you can always find an order to throw them in such that two balls won’t come crashing down on the same beat—which would ruin the act.

If the numbers are all positive, then the answer to Graham’s question is obviously yes: The sums will always grow larger as you add more numbers. Similarly, if there are both positive and negative numbers in the mix, the answer is also known to be yes. But what if the numbers live in a finite world—like numbers wrapped around a clock, which repeat after a certain count?

That’s what Graham wanted to know. He conjectured that the answer should still be yes. It often happens, he figured, that even when dealing with rigid constraints, you can still find enough flexibility to construct special patterns or structures—just as it’s usually possible to find a valid sudoku board or Latin square (another kind of puzzle) despite their many rules. “It fits nicely in all these questions about designs and about very symmetric structures,” said Noga Alon, a mathematician at Princeton University. But for decades, no one could prove Graham’s intuition to be true.

That changed recently, when several young mathematicians picked up the balls. In a proof that spanned four papers and various fields of mathematics, they finally resolved Graham’s rearrangement conjecture. The final paper, by Lisa Sauermann of the University of Bonn and Huy Tuan Pham of the University of Chicago, appeared in February 2026, officially closing the problem.

Across the papers, one theme prevailed: the power of randomness to draw out patterns. As Alon put it, “It’s the power of collaboration, the power of the young generation, the power of probabilistic methods” that solved the problem.

Alp Müyesser, a mathematician at the University of Oxford, often finds himself drawn to problems whose solutions need two ingredients: a random process and something extra as well. After solving one such problem in 2022 while he was still a graduate student, he encountered Graham’s conjecture and realized that his just-finished proof could help there, too.

The conjecture is set in the world of clock arithmetic. You start by placing the whole numbers on a number line, then you wrap the line around the face of a clock so that the numbers repeat after some prime number, p. Say p is 7, for instance. In this setting, 0, 7, 14, and all other multiples of 7 are equivalent—meaning that you can add two positive numbers (like 3 and 4) and get zero.

Graham asked the following: If you pick any set of nonzero numbers off this number line (for any p), can you always rearrange them so that the partial sums you get are all different?

The challenge depends on how big your set is compared to p. The more numbers you pick, the more sums there are to manage. But if you choose fewer numbers, there will be fewer ways to rearrange them. These different cases inspire different approaches.

Müyesser, along with his former adviser, Alexey Pokrovskiy of University College London, tackled the case where your set includes almost every possible number up to p. With sets this large, it can be extremely hard to construct a valid ordering. But it turned out that starting with a random ordering can bring you most of the way there.

“Computer scientists often call this a ‘finding the hay in the haystack’ problem,” Müyesser said. You might know that lots of good orderings are out there, but actually finding one is hard. “If you do it randomly, it’s likely going to work, but it’s hard to explicitly describe what the solution is supposed to look like.”

Müyesser and Pokrovskiy needed to ensure that no sequence of numbers anywhere in the ordering added up to zero. Otherwise, adding those numbers to the previous partial sum would repeat that sum.

A completely random ordering might have a few of these troublesome sequences. So Müyesser and Pokrovskiy first set aside a few specially chosen numbers from the set, then randomly scrambled the rest. They scanned their random ordering for any problems; if they came across an interval that added up to zero, they could insert one of the spare numbers to change it. In 2022, they posted their solution, though it was hidden in a paper that focused on applying the same technique to a more general problem.

A couple of years later, Noah Kravitz of Oxford, unaware of Müyesser and Pokrovskiy’s solution, stumbled on Graham’s conjecture in an online archive of unsolved problems. “I saw there was an open problem, and I was like, it’s embarrassing for humanity that we don’t know this,” Kravitz said. “This situation just had to be rectified.”

He decided to approach the conjecture from the opposite end. Together with Benjamin Bedert of Oxford, he considered the case where the set of numbers is tiny compared to p—for instance, Alon said, if you have a set of 100 numbers where p is 1 billion.

Kravitz and Bedert solved Graham’s conjecture for those cases and posted their proof in September 2024. Müyesser saw it and reached out, sharing his own work; the three of them (plus two other colleagues) then teamed up to extend Müyesser’s original approach.

“It was a pretty unlikely combination of people,” Kravitz said. He and Müyesser come from two areas of combinatorics that don’t typically collaborate. “Different sections have completely different techniques,” he said.

Their paper, which they posted in August 2025, handled more cases where the set of numbers is relatively large compared to p. But between those cases and the small-set cases that Kravitz and Bedert had covered, a gap remained. No one could figure out what to do about medium-size sets, such as those that include roughly half as many numbers as p. “Our methods didn’t work there, and there were clear reasons that they would not have worked,” Müyesser said.

It seemed as though research on the problem might enter another long hiatus. Then, in February 2026, a surprise appeared online.

Lisa Sauermann and Huy Tuan Pham were old friends. The two mathematicians had met in 2015 at Stanford University, where Sauermann was a graduate student and Pham an undergraduate. Today they live on different continents—Sauermann in Bonn, Germany, and Pham in Chicago. But a conference in Germany in September 2025 provided a rare chance for them to share a chalkboard again, and afterward Pham followed Sauermann to Bonn for a short visit. All they needed was a problem to work on.

At the conference, they heard two talks on Graham’s conjecture by mathematicians who had attempted but failed to bridge the gap. They were intrigued. And as it later turned out, Sauermann had encountered a closely related problem in the International Mathematical Olympiad as a high school student. She solved it correctly, and by the time she finished high school, she’d won a gold medal in the prestigious competition four times. (Most likely, it was Chung who placed the problem on that year’s exam, as she was on the committee that wrote the questions, and she frequently took inspiration from Graham’s many puzzles.)

By the end of their three-day visit, Sauermann and Pham had a plan for how to crack the case.

It hinged on a technically demanding method called anti-concentration. Here, an anti-concentration statement asserts that some event has a particularly low chance of happening. But the mechanics of proving these kinds of statements are so intricate that, though Kravitz and others were aware that such an anti-concentration approach might succeed, “we just hadn’t had the guts to actually try it,” he said.

First, though, Sauermann and Pham began the way their predecessors had. They randomly reordered their set of numbers and came up with a procedure to fix any problems—that is, any sequences that add up to zero. Any time they found a zero-sum sequence, they swapped out the last number in the sequence with another one.

This procedure often went without a hitch. But three types of “bad events” would cause it to fail. One: A zero-sum sequence might occur toward the end of the entire arrangement; then there would be no other numbers to swap in. Two: Many zero-sum sequences might appear too close together, making it impossible to fix them all. And three: Fixing one bad sequence might create another zero-sum sequence down the line.

Sauermann and Pham hoped to prove, using anti-concentration, that each of these bad events was sufficiently unlikely. Then there would have to be a way to rearrange the set of numbers to satisfy the conjecture.

To do this, the duo used Fourier analysis—an area of math that lets you rewrite functions as sums of simple waves—to show that in general, when you add up random sets of numbers, no one sum is especially likely to appear. They then used this insight to carefully estimate the probability that each bad event would occur, ultimately showing that the total chance of getting a bad event was less than 100 percent. That was enough to settle the conjecture.

A few months after their stint in Germany, Sauermann and Pham posted their 27-page proof online. They had shown not only that a satisfactory rearrangement was always possible, but that a random ordering could be rearranged to eliminate bad events at least 90% of the time—a massive success rate.

The mathematicians who had previously worked on the problem were surprised to see the remaining case closed so quickly. “Their approach is just completely different,” Müyesser said.

Together, the four papers prove Graham’s conjecture for sets of all sizes. But they all assume that p is very large; though no one has calculated its exact value, think along the lines of 10 raised to the 100th power. To mathematicians, that’s fine—the salient point is that you’re working in the setting of clock arithmetic. But another aspect of the problem technically remains unsolved—you might still try to resolve the conjecture for all p. And if you want to use the result to choreograph a real juggling routine, you’re out of luck: To correspond to such a large p, the routine would have to be much too long.

The proof confirms that even within these strange, limited number settings, “there are some nice structures that always exist,” Alon said. You can always achieve some degree of flexibility, shuffling the numbers in your set around to avoid revisiting the same partial sums.

“To pose a good problem is really an art,” Chung said. “I think Ron would be extremely happy to see the problem solved.”

entries.title: The Apple MacBook Pro M5 is on Sale, and a Top MacBook to Buy Right Now
entries.summary: Apple announced an updated 14-inch MacBook Pro with the latest M6 chip. But with the M5 model on sale, I’m not sure the M6 is worth the upgrade.
entries.content:
Last month, Apple refreshed the 14-inch MacBook Pro with the latest M6 chip. It's powerful, has great battery life, and the mini-LED screen is bright. There are all kinds of great attributes about this laptop, but you probably shouldn't buy it. At least, not right now.

While the updated M6 is a perfectly capable laptop in its own right, it fits a bit awkwardly into the current lineup of MacBooks. It's identical to the previous-gen M5 model, which came out in late 2025. But here's the problem: Despite having the exact same laptop specs (save for the chip difference), you can currently get the M5 for $200 less on Amazon and Walmart.

If you're thinking that upgrading from the M5 to the M6 must be worth $200, I'm not so sure. The M6 comes with two additional CPU and GPU cores, which is the origin of most of its gains. While that's not nothing, it's one of the smaller gen-over-gen Apple Silicon performance bumps in the past six years. The main difference is in AI performance, thanks to the second 16-core Neural Engine and faster memory bandwidth on the M6. In day-to-day work—or even in content creation workflows—I just don't think the difference will be very noticeable between the two models. That's especially true since the base 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't a true pro laptop in terms of performance. It uses the same M5 chip that's in the MacBook Air and iPad Pro, after all. The only other real difference is in wireless connectivity, where you get the bump to Wi-Fi 7 with the M6 model.

If you're going to buy the 14-inch MacBook Pro M5, though, you should also be considering the 15-inch MacBook Air. The main difference between these two laptops is the quality of the display. The mini-LED panel on the MacBook Pro is much brighter and more colorful, allowing for some very impressive HDR performance. It also has more ports, such as HDMI and an SD card slot. My favorite small feature is its USB-C ports on both sides of the laptop, allowing for charging from either direction.

The 15-inch MacBook Air is actually on sale today, too. The model with 16 GB of memory and a terabyte of storage is at its lowest price since June: $1,549. That's $150 off Apple's retail price.

So, whether you opt for the thinner 15-inch MacBook Air M5 or the 14-inch MacBook Pro M5 with its better screen, you have great deals to enjoy. The same just can't be said as of now for the M6 MacBook Pro.

entries.title: 6 Best Touchscreen Gloves (2026) Knitted, Waterproof, Leather, and More
entries.summary: We braved the cold to answer a modern dilemma: Can you keep your hands warm and use a smartphone at the same time?
entries.content:
Featured in this article

The obvious way to keep the extreme cold from nipping at your fingers is to slip on a pair of toasty gloves. But traditional gloves don’t play nicely with our smartphones. Why stab futilely at your device when you can snag a good pair of touchscreen gloves?

These types of gloves use materials or fingertip technology that work with touchscreens, but some are better than others. I tested each pair in this guide with my phone—answering calls, browsing the web, and sending text messages—and also considered comfort, grip, and warmth, using them in 30- to 40-degree Fahrenheit weather. These are my favorites.

Updated November 2026: I added gloves from Cross Point Gear, removed some older discontinued gloves, and updated links and prices.

Adjust Your Phone’s Settings

Before diving in, I strongly recommend increasing your phone’s touchscreen sensitivity. Here’s how:

On an Android phone: Go to Settings, Display and touch, Touch sensitivity, and toggle Increased sensitivity on. These settings may vary slightly on different Android phones.

On an iPhone: Go to Settings, Accessibility, Touch, tap Haptic Touch or 3D & Haptic Touch, then select Fast. You should also consider tweaking some of the settings in Settings, Accessibility, Touch, and Touch Accommodations.

Other Touchscreen Gloves I Tested

Some of the touchscreen gloves we tried fell short of a recommendation for one reason or another.

Verloop Twist Knit Touchscreen Gloves for $35: Gloves don’t have to be gray, as these vibrant, eye-catching, fun color combinations prove. I tested the Twist Knit Touchscreen Gloves in magenta and cobalt, and they proved an instant hit with my daughter. The tips of the thumb, index finger, and middle finger are touchscreen-friendly. She found it easy to swipe around and even type with some practice, but you need a snug fit to type at speed and use your thumbs. These gloves are cozy, with ribbed cuffs, and they are machine washable but not waterproof.

Black Diamond Lightweight Screentap Gloves for $40: Thin gloves can maintain dexterity while still providing some warmth. A suede patch on the palm provides great padding when you hold an umbrella or steering wheel. It’s easy to use the touchscreen with my thumb, so these are great for one-handed use, and I can type at close to normal speed. These gloves also have an elasticated wrist for a snug fit and a plastic clip to join them when they’re off, so you never lose one. They’re not especially warm, and they feel a little slippery.

Graphene-X All Rounder Bio-X Gloves for $119: With a classy look, high-tech graphene material on the back, and plant-based bio leather on the palm and fingers, these gloves are certainly unique. They’re comfy too, but they completely failed to keep my hands warm. The touchscreen material works, and I had no trouble tapping and swiping, but the joins and squared-off fingertips made it almost impossible to type accurately.

Trendoux Winter Gloves for $8: These affordable gloves have tips on the index fingers and thumbs that work with touchscreens, but the seams on the inside make them tricky to type with and a little uncomfortable. They are slim, so not especially warm, but the finish is smooth and water-resistant, with rubbery anti-slip dots on the palm and other fingers. I like the clip for snapping them together when you take them off.

Try These Instead

Maybe you already have non-touchscreen gloves you love, or you simply don’t fancy any of our picks. There are a couple of alternatives worth considering:

A stylus: It may seem old school, but a stylus allows you to use your phone accurately without taking your gloves off and will work with any smartphone or gloves. The Bargains Depot 2-in-1 Stylus ($9) worked well in our testing.

A handwarmer: If you brave the cold gloveless or use one of our thinner picks above, you might want to have a rechargeable handwarmer waiting in your pocket. My favorite is the VQ Rechargeable 10,000-mAh Power Bank Hand Warmer (£30), but it’s only available in the UK. Folks in the US can find a ton of similar options on Amazon.

entries.title: World Models Will Soon Be Inescapable. Here’s What You Need to Know
entries.summary: Moving AI from text to 3D space, world models simulate real-world physics to teach robots and autonomous cars how to navigate reality.
entries.content:
It’s 2016, and you’re wandering around the neighborhood at dusk. On the prowl, you’re swiping on a smartphone to catch that elusive Snorlax and grow your collection in Pokémon Go. You, alongside hundreds of millions of other players, are enjoying a mixed-reality game built around lovable characters. What you don’t realize is that these scans of your environment will one day help robots navigate obstacles and interact with objects.

Niantic, the creator of Pokémon Go, sold the game last year and pivoted hard into one of Silicon Valley’s buzziest AI topics right now: world models. “We’re very much about reconstructing the real world,” says Brian McClendon, Niantic Spatial’s chief technology officer. He hopes to leverage its trove of world data to build replicas. Unlike the text-based nature of large language models, world models use visual inputs and can generate digital environments that simulate physics.

This software is poised to seep into everyday life, without you necessarily ever interacting directly with world models. 2027 could be a major year for the expansion of home robotics and driverless cars, both of which are bolstered by advances in world models. It’s time to better understand how these bots think.

“So with a language model, you have a sentence, and it will predict the next word in the sentence,” says Oliver Cameron, the CEO of Odyssey, an AI lab focused on world models. “With a world model, you give it a visual state of the world, an image, and it will then predict the next visual state of the world.” These 3D generations can be used as digital training grounds. “They’re simulations, but they look and feel real,” he says.

McClendon sees these world models as helping robots practice without physical movement or being in intended environments. He says someone could take photos of where the robot is intended to function, generate a 3D model, and then let the software run “millions of simulations” to train the robot on the space’s parameters.

It’s not just humanoid robots that could use simulated practice; driverless cars also improve using world models. Without a human behind the wheel, split-second software reactions are paramount.

“Importantly, a world model must be able to react to the actions that we take in the world, and so it must understand physics, cause and effect, and how other objects and people change their actions in response to our own,” says Jamie Shotton, chief scientist at Wayve, which builds world models designed for cars.

Wayve’s generative world model is powered, in part, by dashcam footage. The startup uses it to recreate hazardous roads and other unsafe conditions that would not be practical to test in real life.

Beyond physical applications, developers are also analyzing how world models could impact video games. Since physics and 3D rendering are core to video games, major players like Tencent are investing in their own world models.

You can expect large AI companies, like Google, to keep boasting about their latest world-model improvements. Investors are also throwing money at insurgent big names in computer science that are turning their attention to the technology. Yann LeCun, Meta’s former chief AI scientist, raised over a billion dollars recently to fund his Advanced Machines Intelligence startup. Additionally, famed Stanford computer scientist Fei-Fei Li launched a startup in 2024 called World Labs, which AMD acquired this year for over $8 billion.

Even if you plan on avoiding autonomous cars and domestic bots altogether, world models are already warping the labor market behind the scenes. To simulate our physical world, AI labs need real people to record it. Earlier this year, I strapped an iPhone to my forehead and recorded hours of videos in my apartment. I recorded my hands folding laundry, washing dishes, and pouring Diet Coke, selling the video data through an app for a fairly measly payout. As more companies attempt to build better world models, even more gig work may demand this kind of data collection.

Between chasing virtual monsters in 2016 and selling videos of my chores in 2026, these systems are ingesting more and more of my physical life. Now I can’t stop picturing the digital ghost of some humanoid robot trapped inside a simulation of my bedroom, endlessly folding my boxers with its metallic claws—getting slightly better with every pass. I’m sorry I didn’t tidy up first.

entries.title: The Fridge-Hacking Spree Is an Internet-of-Things Wake-Up Call
entries.summary: Escalating hacks affecting blood labs and grocery stores show the very real risks to critical infrastructure that come from basic security lapses involving internet-connected devices.
entries.content:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Amid an onslaught of AI vulnerability discovery and AI-assisted hacking, some of the most consequential critical infrastructure attacks this year may have little to do with the technology at all—instead providing a stark reminder that cybersecurity fundamentals are still key to digital defense.

Three sites in France that handle blood and plasma bags were briefly impacted this week by widespread attacks on vulnerable internet-connected refrigerators. On Wednesday, the Établissement Français du Sang (EFS) confirmed that cold rooms storing blood were “raised to very high temperatures” on November 2. The blood samples, thankfully, weren’t altered or damaged, the EFS said, because the organization’s alarm facilities and staff quickly detected the changes and implemented fail-safe measures.

The incident, however, comes amid a wave of cyberattacks in recent days affecting supermarket chains in at least 11 European countries that also drastically increased the temperatures of their refrigerators. Pictures from across the continent show huge volumes of food being trashed following the spikes. Similar fridge attacks in October affected hundreds of French stores that were forced to throw away food. And in August, roughly six commissaries and grocery stores on United States military bases suffered similar incidents resulting in spoiled food. The Pentagon is investigating the incidents and is collaborating with French law enforcement, Reuters reported last week.

“It's been true for more than a decade now that our dependence on connected technology is growing faster than our collective will to protect it, which has exposed us to accidents, adversaries, and now potentially agents,” says longtime critical infrastructure researcher Josh Corman, who is currently the executive in residence for public safety and resilience at the nonprofit Institute for Security and Technology. “These fragile cold-chain systems are too critical to fail, but we keep experiencing hard lessons.”

It is still unclear who is behind the incidents and whether the attacks are all connected or being carried out by multiple actors. The first recent wave of attacks against French supermarkets last month appears to have been caused by attackers exploiting unpatched refrigeration controllers exposed to the internet—including software versions that allegedly used weak passwords formulated based on the date.

Many of the hacks stem from attackers exploiting vulnerabilities in temperature controllers made by the Danish firm Danfoss, and researchers say the attacks would not have been particularly difficult to pull off. Danfoss did not return WIRED’s request for comment.

In other statements, Danfoss said impacted systems “were running outdated firmware” and urged customers to keep products updated. In an alert on Thursday addressing the rash of incidents, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said attacks could exploit flaws in cold storage systems via authentication bypasses, arbitrary code injections, and weak configurations. Experts have long warned about the dire threats to critical infrastructure posed by these types of weaknesses in so-called internet-of-things devices.

Russian hacktivists tried to claim responsibility for some of the attacks but did not provide credible evidence. Still, some researchers see signs that Russia-based actors may have been involved in at least some of the incidents. The Kremlin this week denied involvement. In other cases, researchers have found potential ties to Iran-linked actors. NextGov/FCW reported last week that unnamed US officials suspect Iran-linked attackers may have been behind the freezer attacks on US military bases, though they noted that the investigation is still ongoing.

This type of refrigerator/freezer attack is not new. Back in 2022, 16 supermarkets in Russia were targeted at the start of the country’s full-scale war with Ukraine. That year, 40 stores in Israel were similarly attacked, according to a 2025 report by Danfoss.

“Many businesses use older technology while the systems become increasingly connected,” Sweden’s National Cyber Security Center pointed out in a recent advisory about the freezer attacks, noting that companies should inventory which of their devices are connected to the internet, disconnect them whenever possible, and make sure they are kept access-controlled, patched, and monitored if they must be connected.

entries.title: Best Wi-Fi Routers (2026): My Honest Picks After Testing 50+
entries.summary: Don’t suffer the buffer. These WIRED-tested home routers will deliver reliable internet across your home, whatever your needs or budget.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

The humble router is an essential fixture in every home. Benefits extend to everything from streaming movies and online gaming to video calls. Most people can get by just fine with a single Wi-Fi router, and I’ve collected recommendations to suit different needs, spaces, and budgets. I have tested all of these in my busy family home, which is full of Netflix-addicted gamers.

After testing more than 50 routers (some have since been discontinued or removed, but many are reviewed on this page), the Asus RT-BE58U is the best Wi-Fi router for most people, especially thanks to its affordable price. I have plenty of alternatives to suit different households and budgets though, including a mesh Wi-Fi option if dead zones plague you.

Make sure to check out our Best Mesh Wi-Fi Routers guide for larger homes. If you’re confused about terminology, my How to Buy a Router guide can help, along with my explainer on mesh systems versus single routers.

Note: The FCC’s foreign-made router ban announced in March may stop any company that doesn’t secure an exemption (Conditional Approval) from selling new routers in the US, however, existing routers can continue to be sold (everything listed here). They can also be updated with new firmware, at least until January 1, 2029. So far, Netgear, Eero, and Asus, among others (here’s the full list), have secured a Conditional Approval.

Updated November 2026: I added the Asus ROG Rapture BN98 Pro as the best Wi-Fi 8 router and the TP-Link Archer 8 Ultra to Other Routers I Tested and Liked.

Compare Top 8 Wi-Fi Routers
